tagline: Lava fields, a green valley and sugar harbors below Mauna Loa.
intro: Highway 11 carries the Kaʻū Scenic Byway across relatively new lava, into the green Waiʻōhinu Valley and down toward the ocean. The drive ranges from sea level to more than 4,000 feet, with forest, ocean views and volcanic terrain along the way. Hawaiʻi Tourism Authority describes this 54-mile scenic byway through its lava fields, Honuʻapo Overlook and Punaluʻu Black Sand Beach. The Kaʻū Chamber of Commerce sponsors it.

Travel between this coast and the volcano predates the scenic designation. Hotelkeeper Peter Lee built a road across the Kaʻū Desert to bring visitors from Punaluʻu to the volcano. At Honuʻapo, a wharf built in 1878–1883 served what became the principal harbor for shipping Kaʻū sugar. Inland, Pāhala became the administrative center of the Kaʻū Sugar Company; its mill was the island’s last sugar mill to close, in 1996.

Begin at Mānuka State Park and cross the western slopes toward the national park’s Kahuku section. Beyond Kahuku, the road winds into Waiʻōhinu Valley before descending toward Honuʻapo Bay. Continue past the flat-topped Nīnole Hills, Punaluʻu and the Pāhala turnoff. The eastern slopes open toward Mauna Loa’s summit as the byway rises to the main entrance of Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park.

moments.title: Honuʻapo
moments.text: The bay below Honuʻapo Overlook was once Kaʻū’s principal sugar-shipping harbor. Its wharf was built between 1878 and 1883. Sugar processing also concentrated here: when the Nāʻālehu mill wore out around 1911, a new central mill at Honuʻapo took over grinding the cane. Honuʻapo’s mill closed in 1972, and its workers transferred to Pāhala. Nāʻālehu, Honuʻapo, Hīlea and Kaʻalaiki had been plantation villages; by 1928 they were consolidated into Nāʻālehu. The former harbor area is now Whittington Beach Park. Traces of harbor structures survive there, with views along the shoreline toward Nāʻālehu and close views of Honuʻapo pond.
moments.notice: Former harbor structures remain at Whittington Beach Park.

moments.title: Punaluʻu Beach
moments.text: Punaluʻu’s black sand is basalt, formed as lava entered the ocean, exploded and cooled. Hawksbill and green turtles frequent the beach and can often be seen basking on the sand. Fresh water also enters the beach underground. The coast includes brackish pools linked to the sea beneath the surface. Their water levels change with the tides despite having no surface connection to the ocean. Native shrimp travel between these pools through underground cracks, another connection between the volcanic shore and the water beneath it. Red seaweed grows on the bay’s coral-encrusted rocks and is a favorite food of green turtles.
moments.notice: Black basalt sand forms the beach; turtles can often be seen basking there.

moments.title: Kaʻū Desert
moments.text: Footprints preserved in volcanic ash record people crossing the Kaʻū Desert during Kīlauea’s 1790 eruption. They were once thought to belong only to warriors returning from battle with Keoua Kuahuula’s army. Research indicates that a variety of people used this area for hundreds of years. The landscape is made mostly of lava remnants, ash, sand and gravel. Despite its name, annual rainfall exceeds 39 inches; rain mixing with volcanic sulfur dioxide forms acid rain that inhibits plant growth. Water also evaporates quickly here, and the soil formed from volcanic fragments is highly permeable.
